It sounds like you are trying to remember a few specific items used in gardening and indoor planting, or perhaps a particular type of self-watering pot system! 
Here is what those specific clues point to: 
1. The Thing in Plant Stuff to Check Water Level
The floating device you see sticking out of planter pots is a mechanical water level indicator or buoyancy float gauge. 
  • How it works: It consists of a plastic tube containing a lightweight foam or plastic floater/buoy attached to a red or white indicator stick. As you pour water into the reservoir, the buoy rises, pushing the stick up to show you when the tub is full. 
2. "Those Pellets, Those Terracotta"
Those round, brown, baked clay balls used in planters are called LECA (Lightweight Expanded Clay Aggregate), often just referred to as clay pebbles, hydroton, or terracotta pellets. 
  • How they are used: They are highly porous, semi-buoyant pellets used as a growing medium in hydroponics, or placed at the bottom of deep planter tubs to assist with drainage, aeration, and moisture control. 
Putting it Together: Sub-Irrigation / Self-Watering Pots
When you combine a water level float gauge, a water reservoir tub, and terracotta LECA pellets, you are looking at a sub-irrigation planter (often popularized by brands like Lechuza).

htmlChunks:
Moving from gardening equipment to Augmented Reality (AR) and Spatial Computing, you are highlighting the core foundational systems used to lock virtual objects into physical spaces. 
Here is how Spatial Anchors and ARCore Cloud Anchors work, and how they relate to your memory terms: 
1. Spatial Anchors (The Broad Concept)
A Spatial Anchor is a general industry term for a "digital bookmark" tied to a specific point in the physical world. 
  • The "Memory" aspect: When an AR headset or phone looks at a room, it uses cameras and sensors to build a local 3D point cloud (a map of visual features like table corners and wall textures). A spatial anchor remembers its exact position relative to those physical features. 
  • Platforms like Meta Horizon OS, Apple visionOS, and Microsoft Azure all use their own variations of Spatial Anchors to ensure that a virtual object (like a digital TV on your wall) stays in the exact same spot across different app sessions. 
2. ARCore Cloud Anchors (Google’s Solution)
ARCore Cloud Anchors are Google's specific implementation of spatial anchors designed for multi-user and cross-platform (Android & iOS) shared AR experiences. 
  • Hosting (Saving the Memory): When you place a virtual object on a real table, ARCore maps the surrounding physical features and uploads that spatial data to Google’s servers. The cloud endpoint processes it and generates a unique Cloud Anchor ID. 
  • Resolving (Recalling the Memory): You share that ID with a friend. When their phone camera points at the same table, their device downloads the anchor data, matches its local environment with the cloud data, and resolves the anchor. Boom: both of you see the exact same virtual object in the exact same physical position. 
  • Persistence: Modern implementations of ARCore Cloud Anchors allow these anchors to persist from 1 to 365 days, meaning you can leave a virtual sticky note in a room and find it there months later.

When you connect spatial anchors and ARCore Cloud Anchors to the concept of a Memory Palace (the ancient Method of Loci), you bridge classic cognitive science with modern spatial computing [The "Memory" aspect]. 
An AR headset mapping a room to drop a digital anchor operates exactly like a human brain building a digital Memory Palace. 
The Brain vs. AR: How They Mirror Each Other
ConceptThe Memory Palace (Human Brain)Spatial Anchors / ARCore (Spatial Computing)
The BlueprintYou mentally visualize a familiar environment, like your childhood home or school.The device uses cameras and LiDAR to map physical visual features (table corners, wall textures) into a 3D point cloud.
Placing the ObjectYou mentally place a vivid memory cue (e.g., a giant neon lemon) on your living room couch.You place a 3D digital asset (e.g., a virtual TV) in the room, creating a Spatial Anchor at that exact 3D coordinate.
Retrieving the InfoYou mentally "walk" through the rooms to find and recall the item you left on the couch.You point your phone at the room. ARCore resolves the anchor, matching live camera frames to the saved cloud map to render the object.

For centuries, building a Memory Palace required intense visualization and mental effort. AR completely flips this. 
Developers and users now use AR to build persistent, physical Memory Palaces in the real world: 
  • Visual Study Spaces: You can drop permanent, floating digital note cards, 3D anatomy models, or timelines in specific corners of your actual bedroom using persistent cloud anchors. 
  • Contextual Triggers: When you enter your office, your AR glasses recognize the spatial map, resolve the anchors, and instantly pull up your digital to-do boards right next to your computer monitor.
